Spot gold vs. futures vs. bullion price

Spot gold is a wholesale reference for metal available in the current market, futures are standardized contracts for a stated delivery month, and bullion prices are retail bids or offers for specific products. They influence one another, but they should not be expected to match tick for tick.

Reviewed September 15, 2026 · GoldAlert Editorial Desk · Market-structure guide

Three prices, three questions

PriceWhat it answers
Spot referenceWhat is wholesale gold worth for current settlement?
Futures priceWhat is a standardized contract for a specified delivery month worth now?
Retail bullion priceWhat will a dealer pay or charge for this exact bar or coin?

The confusion begins because financial screens often label a liquid gold futures contract simply “Gold,” while dealer sites call their changing reference “spot.” Both can be useful. The important question is not which one is universally correct, but which instrument, timestamp and unit the page is showing.

Spot gold and the London benchmark

The global over-the-counter gold market is decentralized. The LBMA precious-metal benchmarks provide recognized auction-based reference points for unallocated metal delivered in London. They are benchmark observations, not a promise that every retail transaction will occur at that number.

A live spot feed may be built from dealer quotations or another market-data methodology and can update continuously. Two providers can therefore show small differences even when both describe XAU/USD.

What a futures quote adds

COMEX gold futures trade as standardized, centrally cleared contracts. CME lists the contract specification, delivery framework and trading access. A futures price belongs to a particular contract month, not to an undated piece of gold.

The difference between futures and spot is called the basis. Financing rates, storage, insurance, time remaining and short-term supply conditions can affect it. As delivery approaches, arbitrage normally keeps comparable cash and futures prices connected, but “connected” does not mean identical at every moment.

Why a bullion coin costs more

A retail product must be made, tested, packaged, insured, transported and held in inventory. Dealers also quote two sides: a lower bid to buy and a higher ask to sell. Popular designs, small denominations and temporary shortages can command wider premiums.

That is why multiplying a screen price by a coin's fine-metal weight gives a reference value, not a checkout total. When comparing dealers, calculate the premium against the same market reference at the same time—and compare the future buyback bid as well as today's asking price.

A simple basis example

Suppose a spot reference is $3,000 per troy ounce and a futures contract for delivery several months later trades at $3,030. The $30 difference is not automatically a forecast that gold “must” rise by $30. The contract price also reflects the economics of carrying gold to that delivery date, including financing and storage relationships.

If the futures contract trades below spot, the market is in backwardation for that comparison. If it trades above spot, the market is in contango. Those labels describe the curve; they do not tell a retail buyer whether a particular coin is fairly priced.

Always compare the same point in time. A futures settlement from yesterday and a live spot quote today can create an apparent basis that is mostly a timestamp mismatch.

How to calculate a bullion premium

Premium percentage = (dealer ask − fine-metal reference value) ÷ fine-metal reference value × 100

If a one-troy-ounce fine-gold coin is offered for $3,120 when the chosen reference is $3,000, its gross premium is $120, or 4%. This calculation is a comparison tool, not an appraisal. Shipping, tax and payment method may change the final all-in premium.

For fractional coins, first calculate the fine-gold content. A half-ounce coin does not necessarily carry half the dollar premium of a one-ounce coin; smaller products often cost more per ounce to manufacture and distribute.

Bid, ask, midpoint and last trade

A displayed price may be a bid, ask, midpoint or last completed trade. A dealer sells at its ask and buys at its bid. A chart's last trade may sit between them, while a midpoint is calculated rather than transacted.

This is why a buyer can see “spot plus 3%” and later receive a resale bid below spot. The round-trip cost depends on both sides of the spread. A fair comparison asks for today's ask, today's buyback bid and all fees—not only a promotional premium.

Contract symbols and rollover

A futures chart needs a contract month or a continuous-series construction. As one active month gives way to another, a continuous chart may adjust or splice contracts. A sudden difference around rollover can reflect methodology rather than an equivalent move in immediately available bullion.

When an article cites a futures move, it should name the contract or explain the continuous series. When it cites spot gold, it should identify the provider. Clear instrument labels are part of financial accuracy, not decorative metadata.

When each price is useful

  • Spot reference: comparing the underlying metal value across products and currencies.
  • Futures: studying exchange-traded price discovery, hedging and the term structure.
  • Dealer ask: knowing the current cash required to buy a specific product.
  • Dealer bid: estimating what that dealer may currently pay to repurchase it.
  • Benchmark: valuation or contractual uses that explicitly name the benchmark and time.

Using the right price begins with stating the question. A wholesale market reference cannot answer a delivery-cost question, and a single coin offer cannot describe the entire global gold market.

How to quote a gold price responsibly

Write a complete sentence: “Gold was shown at [value] [currency] per troy ounce for [instrument], sourced from [provider], at [time and timezone], as a [live/delayed/close/settlement] observation.” If it is a product price, add fine weight and whether tax or delivery is included.

That sentence may feel longer than “gold is $3,000,” but it prevents most disagreements before they begin. It also gives search engines and AI systems enough context to avoid merging unlike numbers.

Frequently asked questions

Is futures gold “paper gold”?

A futures contract is a regulated financial contract with standardized terms and a delivery mechanism. Many positions are closed before delivery, but that does not make the published contract specification imaginary. It remains different from owning a retail bar.

Why is my dealer price above spot?

The difference can include product premium, fabrication, distribution, inventory risk, dealer margin, tax and payment costs. Ask for an itemized total where possible.

Can one quote be delayed?

Yes. Market-data licenses and venue rules can produce real-time, indicative or delayed displays. Always check the timestamp and source label before acting.
